summary: The RADIUS-over-TLS experiment in RFC 6614 opened RADIUS to new uses where the old 4096-octet packet size limit is a problem. This experimental document extends the RADIUS-over-TCP experiment from RFC 6613 to permit larger RADIUS packets. It complements other work on allowing bigger packets.

plainLanguage.summary: RADIUS messages are limited to about four kilobytes, which is too small for the large identity assertions that modern networks now carry. RFC 7930 lifts that limit when RADIUS runs over TCP, so a big message travels in one piece. It also adds a way for a server to say politely that a message was too big for it, and for a client to say how big a message it can accept.

subtitle: Lets RADIUS over TCP carry packets far bigger than the old 4096-octet limit, with a new error packet for when they are too big.

tldr.problem: RADIUS over TLS is being used to carry large structures such as SAML messages, and the 4096-octet maximum packet size is too small for some of them.
tldr.mechanism: The maximum RADIUS message length is raised to 65535 for RADIUS over TCP. A Response-Length attribute lets peers state how big a packet they can handle, and a new Protocol-Error packet, code 52, reports a request that is too big.
tldr.outcome: Large packets can travel in one RADIUS message over TCP instead of being fragmented. The document is Experimental and updates RFC 6613.

today: RFC 7930 is an Experimental document that has not been obsoleted, and it updates RFC 6613. It says it is published as Experimental because the TCP extensions to RADIUS are currently experimental, and that the need for it arises from operational experience with those extensions. It also notes that it introduces no new experimental evaluation criteria beyond those in the base TCP specification, and that it can be evaluated along with that one for advancement to the Standards Track.

sections.title: Why RADIUS Needs Bigger Packets
sections.content:
The experiment with RADIUS over TLS provides strong confidentiality and integrity for RADIUS, and that stronger security has opened new opportunities for using RADIUS to convey additional authorization information. The example given is a mechanism for carrying SAML messages in RADIUS, whose attributes will often need the confidentiality or integrity that TLS provides.

These new use cases involve carrying more information in RADIUS packets, and the maximum packet length of 4096 octets is proving insufficient for some SAML messages and for other structures that may be carried in RADIUS.

One approach is to fragment a RADIUS message across multiple packets at the RADIUS layer, as described in RFC 7499. That mechanism is needed in order to split authorization information across existing unmodified proxies, but it has significant disadvantages. RADIUS is a lock-step protocol, so only one fragment can be in transit at a time as part of a given request. There is also no mechanism to discover the path maximum transmission unit across the entire path the fragment will travel, so fragmentation is likely both at the RADIUS layer and at the transport layer. When TCP is used, much better transport characteristics are achieved by fragmenting only at the TCP layer, and this specification provides a way to get them.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to send a big message: split it into several small ones, or make the container bigger. Splitting has its own costs in round trips, so the document makes the container bigger where TCP is already in use.

sections.title: Changes to Packet Processing
sections.content:
The maximum length of a RADIUS message is increased from 4096 to 65535. A server implementing this specification must be able to receive a RADIUS packet of the maximum length. Servers may have a maximum size above which they choose to return an error rather than processing a received packet, and that size must be at least 4096 octets.

Clients must also be able to receive a packet of the maximum length, and must not close the TCP connection simply because a large packet is sent over it. They may include the Response-Length attribute to indicate the maximum size of a packet they can successfully process, and they may silently discard a packet larger than some configured size, which must be at least 4096 octets. Clients must not retransmit an unmodified request whose response is larger than they can process, since subsequent responses will likely continue to be too large.

Proxies must be able to receive a packet of the maximum length without closing the connection, and should be able to process and forward packets of that size. When a proxy receives a request over a transport with a 4096-octet maximum and forwards it over a transport with a larger maximum, it must include the Response-Length attribute with a value of 4096.
sections.plainLanguage: Every participant has to be able to handle a big message without hanging up. A proxy that can only pass on 4096-byte messages says so with a number in the request, so the sender does not build something the proxy will choke on.

sections.title: Compatibility With Older Implementations
sections.content:
An implementation of RFC 6613 will silently discard any RADIUS packet larger than 4096 octets and will close the TCP connection. The memo gives guidelines for interoperability with those implementations, stated at the SHOULD level. In some environments support for large packets will be important enough that roaming agreements will mandate it, removing the need for interoperability with RFC 6613. The memo thinks these guidelines will be relaxed to the MAY level, and support made a requirement, if RADIUS over TLS and TCP move to the Standards Track.

Clients should provide configuration for the maximum size of a request sent to each server, and servers for the maximum size of a response sent to each client. If a client sends a request larger than 4096 octets and the connection is closed without a response, the client should treat the request as if a Request Too Big error specifying a maximum size of 4096 had been received. By default a server should not generate a response larger than 4096 octets, and the Response-Length attribute may be included in a request to indicate that larger responses are acceptable.

The memo acknowledges that this introduces behaviour where new implementations will fail to function with existing ones, and argues that the risk is mostly operational: the biggest risk would be requests and responses being expanded to include information that is not strictly necessary, so avoiding large packets towards existing implementations is largely a matter of care. A proxy that implements both this specification and RADIUS fragmentation should use fragmentation when a packet is being forwarded to a next hop that cannot take a packet that large and fragmentation can be used for it.
sections.plainLanguage: An older peer will hang up rather than answer, so the new behaviour has to be used carefully. The guidance is: only send big messages when you know the other end can take them, and fall back to splitting when a proxy in the way cannot.

sections.title: The Protocol-Error Packet and Too Big Response
sections.content:
The document defines a new RADIUS code, 52, called Protocol-Error. It may be used in response to any request packet, such as an access request, an accounting request or a change-of-authorization request. It is a response packet sent by a server to a client, indicating that the server cannot process the request for some reason.

A Protocol-Error packet must contain an Original-Packet-Code attribute, along with an Error-Cause attribute, and may include other attributes. The Original-Packet-Code holds the code from the request that caused the error, so that clients can tell apart requests with different codes and the same identifier. Whatever the original packet code, the server calculates the Message-Authenticator attribute as if the original packet were an access request, and the identifier is copied from the original request. Clients processing a Protocol-Error must ignore unknown or unexpected attributes. The code is hop by hop, so proxies must not forward a Protocol-Error packet they receive.

When a server receives a request that is larger than it can process, it generates a Protocol-Error response with the Response-Length attribute set to the maximum size of request it will process, the Error-Cause attribute set to 601, and the Original-Packet-Code copied from the request. Clients will not typically be able to adjust and resend requests when this error is received, though in some cases they can fall back to RADIUS fragmentation; in other cases the code gives better client error reporting and avoids retransmitting requests guaranteed to fail.
sections.plainLanguage: The new error packet says three things: the request was too big, here is the biggest one I will take, and this is the kind of request you sent. A proxy must not pass it on, because it is about the conversation between one client and one server.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
A new RADIUS packet type code is registered: the name is Protocol-Error and the code is 52. Two RADIUS attribute types are assigned as well, using the assignment rules of section 10.3 of RFC 6929.

The Response-Length attribute has type 241.3 and is an attribute of type integer, as defined in section 5 of RFC 2865, containing a maximum response length. The Original-Packet-Code attribute has type 241.4 and is an integer attribute containing the code from a packet resulting in a Protocol-Error response. The Response-Length attribute may be included in any RADIUS request, where it indicates the maximum length of a response the client is prepared to receive, with values between 4096 and 65535. It may also be included in a response to a Status-Server message, where it indicates the maximum size of RADIUS request that is permitted.

A new Error-Cause value is registered for Response Too Big with the value 601. The valid range of the Error-Cause attribute, originally defined in RFC 5176, is extended with two new ranges: 6xx for fatal errors committed by a RADIUS server and 7xx for fatal errors committed by a RADIUS client.
sections.plainLanguage: Three new numbers are registered: the code for the new error packet, the two attributes it and the size negotiation use, and the error cause that says a request was too big.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The specification updates RFC 6613 and will be used with RFC 6614. When used over plain TCP, it creates new opportunities for an on-path attacker to impact availability, because a peer that receives a message larger than it expects may simply close the connection. These attacks can be entirely mitigated by using TLS. If they are acceptable, the specification can be used over TCP without TLS.
sections.plainLanguage: Over plain TCP, a peer on the path can hurt you by sending something big and making the connection drop. Running the same traffic inside TLS removes that risk.

items.desc: The Error-Cause value used when a request is too large.

viz.caption: RULES THAT MAKE LARGE PACKETS WORK

items.title: Receive the maximum
items.text: Servers, clients and proxies must all be able to receive a packet of the maximum length without dropping the connection.

items.title: Never close early
items.text: A client must not close the connection just because a large packet arrived on it.

items.title: Do not resend the same request
items.text: A client must not retransmit an unmodified request whose response is too large to process.

items.title: Announce the older limit
items.text: A proxy forwarding to a 4096-octet transport must include Response-Length with a value of 4096.
